content: 1. Clinical, laboratory, pharmacy, and other data are integrated over time to provide a comprehensive view of patient care. 2. Person-based records are linked with death registry data to ensure accurate tracking of outcomes. 3. Online data systems with unique identifiers enable the tracking and follow-up of individuals across various health services. 4. Sustained investment in system maintenance, hardware, software support, and human resources is essential to ensure the system remains operational. 5. The use of unique identifiers for person-centered monitoring of HIV services is critical for effective care delivery. 6. The pathway to fully implementing unique identifiers and electronic health records does not need to follow a strict sequence, but certain foundational elements must be established before initiating further improvements. 7. The starting point and priorities for implementation depend on findings from situation analyses and the feasibility of implementation. 8. Thailand and the Western Cape Province in South Africa have advanced the use of unique identifiers for person-centered care. 9. In Thailand, all citizens are issued a 13-digit personal identification number (PID) at birth, which is used to link health data across community hospitals, general hospitals, and regional health facilities. 10. The Ministry of the Interior collects data on births and deaths at the district level, while health facilities record treatment and care data for people with HIV. 11. This data is stored in a centralized, web-based Disease Management Information System (DMIS) under the National AIDS Programme, which supports program management and reimbursement through the National Health Security Office (NHSO). 12. The PID links all individual-level information and is encrypted and stored securely in a central database, accessible only to authorized hospital users. 13. The PID also serves as the National AIDS Programme (NAP) number, facilitating the integration of HIV-related data with other health information. 14. In the Western Cape Province, South Africa, the unique identifier system began with existing electronic identification and information systems. 15. A provincial unique patient identifier is electronically linked to hospital information systems, provincial electronic discharge summaries, primary health-care facilities, and laboratory, pharmacy, radiology, and other supporting systems. 16. The long-term goal is to create a longitudinal, citizen-centric health record that integrates existing information with new functionalities, such as electronic prescribing, test result viewing, appointment scheduling, and health analytics. 17. The system progresses from paper records at the facility level to electronic registers at the district level, with data aggregated into a centralized database at the provincial level. 18. This data is used for individual and program management through regular reports on follow-up losses, viral load data, and de-duplication of health records. 19. Interoperability in health care refers to the ability of different systems and software to communicate, exchange data, and use the exchanged information effectively. 20. Interoperable health information systems ensure that all relevant information about an individual can be linked for their benefit over time and across facilities. 21. Data exchange protocols and standards must allow data sharing across clinics, laboratories, hospitals, and pharmacies, regardless of the application used. 22. Open-source systems are increasingly supported for health information systems to enhance interoperability and reduce reliance on proprietary software. 23. Fragmented data systems and legacy software often hinder effective communication between data sources, limiting decision-making capabilities. 24. Interoperability requires standardization at both the technical and semantic levels, ensuring consistent definitions of data elements and indicators. 25. Unique identifiers reduce the risk of breaches in information security by replacing name-based records with anonymized codes. 26. Differentiated access and data security protocols should protect sensitive identifying elements, such as names, addresses, and phone numbers. 27. Electronic health records enable the analysis of individual-level data for program management, improvement, and research purposes. 28. Transitioning from paper-based to electronic systems is a critical step in managing the complexity of individual care and HIV program management. 29. The advanced stage of development involves fully interoperable data systems that link information from various sources, including vital statistics and migration data, to track individuals lost to follow-up. 30. Sustainability in program improvements relies on the ability to track and retain individuals in care and treatment while linking health data consistently over time.
